AI is integrated into CS50 to help students learn and solve problems [1, 11]. The course utilizes a CS50 Duck, an AI-based software tool available at cs50.ai, designed to act like a teaching fellow or teaching assistant [1, 2].

Here's how the AI is used:

*   **Conceptual Help:** The AI can provide conceptual help with computer science concepts [3].
*   **Code Improvement:** It can assist students in writing more efficient code [3]. For example, it can explain highlighted lines of code and advise on code style [1].
*   **Problem Solving:** The AI can help students when they encounter errors or get stuck on assignments by offering explanations and guidance [1, 3]. It aims to guide students to answers without simply giving them outright [1].
*   **24/7 Support:** The AI offers virtual office hours, providing support at any time, which is particularly helpful given students' busy schedules [1].

**Rules for using AI in CS50:**

*   **Prohibition of External AI Tools:** The syllabus states that using AI-based software like ChatGPT, GitHub Copilot, or Bing Chat is not allowed, except for CS50's own AI [1, 2].
*   **CS50 Duck is Allowed:** Students are encouraged to use the CS50 Duck at CS50.ai, which is designed to provide a balanced level of assistance [1, 2].
*   **Proper Citation for Final Projects:** For the final project only, it is acceptable to use AI-based software other than CS50's own, but you still must cite any use of such tools in the comments of your code [7].
*   **Guardrails:** The goal is to provide guardrails so that students are lead to the answers, rather than having the answers handed to them [1, 2].

## [Welcome!](https://cs50.harvard.edu/x/2024/notes/ai/#welcome)

- In computer science and programming circles, *rubber ducking* or *rubber duck debugging* is the act of speaking to an inanimate object to be able to *talk through* a challenging problem.
- Most recently, CS50 created our own rubber duck debugger at [cs50.ai](https://cs50.ai/) , which uses artificial intelligence as a way by which to interact with students to help them with their own challenging problems.
- Students engaging with this tool can begin understanding the potential of what AI can offer the world.

## [Image Generation](https://cs50.harvard.edu/x/2024/notes/ai/#image-generation)

- Numerous AI tools have created the potential for artificially generated images to enter the world.
- Up until recently, most of these tools had numerous tells that might indicate to an observer that an image is AI-generated.
- However, tools are becoming exceedingly good at generating these images.
- Indeed, as technology improves, it will soon be almost, if not entirely, impossible for such images to be detected with the naked eye.
- Software has also gained the ability to mutate individual images within video.

## [ChatGPT](https://cs50.harvard.edu/x/2024/notes/ai/#chatgpt)

- A very well-known bleeding-edge tool is the text generation tool *chatGPT* .
- In CS50, we do not allow the use of ChatGPT. However, we do allow the use of our own rubber duck debugger at [cs50.ai](https://cs50.ai/) .
- In CS50, we leverage the tools of Azure and OpenAI, along with our own vector database that holds very recent information from our most recent lectures and offerings, to provide our rubber duck debugger toll.

## [Prompt Generation](https://cs50.harvard.edu/x/2024/notes/ai/#prompt-generation)

- *Prompt generation* is the way by which an individual can communicate with an AI platform.
- We use a *system prompt* to teach the AI how to interact with users. We teach the AI how to work with students.
- *User prompts* are those provided by users to interact with the AI. With these prompts, students interact with the AI.

# [Final Project](https://cs50.harvard.edu/x/2024/project/#final-project)

The climax of this course is its final project. The final project is your opportunity to take your newfound savvy with programming out for a spin and develop your very own piece of software. So long as your project draws upon this course's lessons, the nature of your project is entirely up to you. You may implement your project in any language(s). You are welcome to utilize infrastructure other than the CS50 Codespace. All that we ask is that you build something of interest to you, that you solve an actual problem, that you impact your community, or that you change the world. Strive to create something that outlives this course.

Inasmuch as software development is rarely a one-person effort, you are allowed an opportunity to collaborate with one or two classmates for this final project. Needless to say, it is expected that every student in any such group contribute equally to the design and implementation of that group's project. Moreover, it is expected that the scope of a two- or three-person group's project be, respectively, twice or thrice that of a typical one-person project. A one-person project, mind you, should entail more time and effort than is required by each of the course's problem sets.

Note that CS50's staff audits submissions to CS50x including this final project. Students found to be in violation of [the Academic Honesty policy](..\syllabus\#academic-honesty) will be removed from the course and deemed ineligible for a certificate. Students who have already completed CS50x, if found to be in violation, will have their CS50 Certificate (and edX Certificate, if applicable) revoked.

## [Ideas](https://cs50.harvard.edu/x/2024/project/#ideas)

- a web-based application using JavaScript, Python, and SQL
- an iOS app using Swift
- a game using Lua with LÖVE
- an Android app using Java
- a Chrome extension using JavaScript
- a command-line program using C
- a hardware-based application for which you program some device
- ...

## [Getting Started](https://cs50.harvard.edu/x/2024/project/#getting-started)

Creating an entire project may seem daunting. Here are some questions that you should think about as you start:

- What will your software do? What features will it have? How will it be executed?
- What new skills will you need to acquire? What topics will you need to research?
- If working with one or two classmates, who will do what?
- In the world of software, most everything takes longer to implement than you expect. And so it's not uncommon to accomplish less in a fixed amount of time than you hope. What might you consider to be a good outcome for your project? A better outcome? The best outcome?

Consider making goal milestones to keep you on track.

If using the CS50 Codespace, create a directory called `project` to store your project source code and other files. You are welcome to develop your project outside of the CS50 Codespace.

For your final project (and your final project only!) it is reasonable to use AI-based software other than CS50's own (e.g., ChatGPT, GitHub Copilot, Bing Chat, et al.), but the essence of the work must still be your own. You've learned enough to use such tools as helpers. Treat such tools as amplifying, not supplanting, your productivity. But you still must cite any use of such tools in the comments of your code.

- your GitHub and edX usernames;
- your city and country;
- and, the date you have recorded this video.

It should then go on to demonstrate your project in action, as with slides, screenshots, voiceover, and/or live action. | What the AI does | Where it lives | How it works | Why it’s useful |
|------------------|----------------|--------------|-----------------|
| **CS 50 Duck** – a “rubber‑duck” chatbot that can explain code, suggest style improvements, answer questions, and even point out errors | Integrated into the CS 50 coding environment (cs50.dev) and the separate web app cs50.ai | The duck is built on top of third‑party large‑language‑model APIs (OpenAI, Microsoft Azure) and a local vector database that stores recent lecture notes and problem‑set material. A *system prompt* teaches the model to behave like a friendly teaching assistant, while the *user prompt* is the student’s question. The model’s responses are flagged as experimental and are reviewed by a human before being shown to the student, so the duck can give quick, helpful feedback without handing out full answers. | It gives students 24/7 “office‑hour” help, lets them debug code line‑by‑line, and encourages them to think through problems rather than just copy answers. |

**Key features of CS 50 Duck**

* Highlight a line of C code → “Explain this line” → instant, model‑generated explanation.  
* Highlight a block of code → “Explain changes” → shows a cleaner, more idiomatic version.  
* Ask a question about a runtime error → receives a natural‑language explanation and possible fixes.  
* The duck’s responses are accompanied by a disclaimer that it is experimental and that a human may review the answer before it is shown.  

These capabilities are described in the course’s policy and in the lecture notes on AI [1][3][9].

## [Welcome!](https://cs50.harvard.edu/x/2024/notes/ai/#welcome)

- In computer science and programming circles, *rubber ducking* or *rubber duck debugging* is the act of speaking to an inanimate object to be able to *talk through* a challenging problem.
- Most recently, CS50 created our own rubber duck debugger at [cs50.ai](https://cs50.ai/) , which uses artificial intelligence as a way by which to interact with students to help them with their own challenging problems.
- Students engaging with this tool can begin understanding the potential of what AI can offer the world.

## [Image Generation](https://cs50.harvard.edu/x/2024/notes/ai/#image-generation)

- Numerous AI tools have created the potential for artificially generated images to enter the world.
- Up until recently, most of these tools had numerous tells that might indicate to an observer that an image is AI-generated.
- However, tools are becoming exceedingly good at generating these images.
- Indeed, as technology improves, it will soon be almost, if not entirely, impossible for such images to be detected with the naked eye.
- Software has also gained the ability to mutate individual images within video.

## [ChatGPT](https://cs50.harvard.edu/x/2024/notes/ai/#chatgpt)

- A very well-known bleeding-edge tool is the text generation tool *chatGPT* .
- In CS50, we do not allow the use of ChatGPT. However, we do allow the use of our own rubber duck debugger at [cs50.ai](https://cs50.ai/) .
- In CS50, we leverage the tools of Azure and OpenAI, along with our own vector database that holds very recent information from our most recent lectures and offerings, to provide our rubber duck debugger toll.

## [Prompt Generation](https://cs50.harvard.edu/x/2024/notes/ai/#prompt-generation)

- *Prompt generation* is the way by which an individual can communicate with an AI platform.
- We use a *system prompt* to teach the AI how to interact with users. We teach the AI how to work with students.
- *User prompts* are those provided by users to interact with the AI. With these prompts, students interact with the AI.

## [CS50.ai](https://cs50.harvard.edu/x/2024/notes/ai/#cs50ai)

- Our [rubber duck debugger](https://cs50.ai/) can provide conceptual help with computer science concepts.
- Further, the [rubber duck debugger](https://cs50.ai/) can help students write more efficient code.
- Additionally, the [rubber duck debugger](https://cs50.ai/) can help when a student is stuck in one of their assignments. For example, students may encounter errors that prevent them from progressing in their assignments. When students hit a wall, they don't have to wait for support staff to be available.

# [Final Project](https://cs50.harvard.edu/x/2024/project/#final-project)

The climax of this course is its final project. The final project is your opportunity to take your newfound savvy with programming out for a spin and develop your very own piece of software. So long as your project draws upon this course's lessons, the nature of your project is entirely up to you. You may implement your project in any language(s). You are welcome to utilize infrastructure other than the CS50 Codespace. All that we ask is that you build something of interest to you, that you solve an actual problem, that you impact your community, or that you change the world. Strive to create something that outlives this course.

Inasmuch as software development is rarely a one-person effort, you are allowed an opportunity to collaborate with one or two classmates for this final project. Needless to say, it is expected that every student in any such group contribute equally to the design and implementation of that group's project. Moreover, it is expected that the scope of a two- or three-person group's project be, respectively, twice or thrice that of a typical one-person project. A one-person project, mind you, should entail more time and effort than is required by each of the course's problem sets.

Note that CS50's staff audits submissions to CS50x including this final project. Students found to be in violation of [the Academic Honesty policy](..\syllabus\#academic-honesty) will be removed from the course and deemed ineligible for a certificate. Students who have already completed CS50x, if found to be in violation, will have their CS50 Certificate (and edX Certificate, if applicable) revoked.

## [Ideas](https://cs50.harvard.edu/x/2024/project/#ideas)

- a web-based application using JavaScript, Python, and SQL
- an iOS app using Swift
- a game using Lua with LÖVE
- an Android app using Java
- a Chrome extension using JavaScript
- a command-line program using C
- a hardware-based application for which you program some device
- ...

## [Getting Started](https://cs50.harvard.edu/x/2024/project/#getting-started)

Creating an entire project may seem daunting. Here are some questions that you should think about as you start:

- What will your software do? What features will it have? How will it be executed?
- What new skills will you need to acquire? What topics will you need to research?
- If working with one or two classmates, who will do what?
- In the world of software, most everything takes longer to implement than you expect. And so it's not uncommon to accomplish less in a fixed amount of time than you hope. What might you consider to be a good outcome for your project? A better outcome? The best outcome?

Consider making goal milestones to keep you on track.

If using the CS50 Codespace, create a directory called `project` to store your project source code and other files. You are welcome to develop your project outside of the CS50 Codespace.

For your final project (and your final project only!) it is reasonable to use AI-based software other than CS50's own (e.g., ChatGPT, GitHub Copilot, Bing Chat, et al.), but the essence of the work must still be your own. You've learned enough to use such tools as helpers. Treat such tools as amplifying, not supplanting, your productivity. But you still must cite any use of such tools in the comments of your code.

**You must complete all three steps!**

#### [Step 1 of 3](https://cs50.harvard.edu/x/2024/project/#step-1-of-3)

Create a short video (that's no more than 3 minutes in length) in which you present your project to the world. Your video **must** begin with an opening section that displays:

- your project's title;
- your name;
- your GitHub and edX usernames;
- your city and country;
- and, the date you have recorded this video.

It should then go on to demonstrate your project in action, as with slides, screenshots, voiceover, and/or live action. See [howtogeek.com/205742/how-to-record-your-windows-mac-linux-android-or-ios-screen](https://www.howtogeek.com/205742/how-to-record-your-windows-mac-linux-android-or-ios-screen/) for tips on how to make a "screencast," though you're welcome to use an actual camera. **How CS 50 uses AI**

| What the AI does | Where it lives | How it works | Why it’s useful |
|------------------|----------------|--------------|-----------------|
| **CS 50 Duck** – a “rubber‑duck” chatbot that can explain code, suggest style improvements, answer questions, and even point out errors | Integrated into the CS 50 coding environment (cs50.dev) and the separate web app cs50.ai | The duck is built on top of third‑party large‑language‑model APIs (OpenAI, Microsoft Azure) and a local vector database that stores recent lecture notes and problem‑set material. A *system prompt* teaches the model to behave like a friendly teaching assistant, while the *user prompt* is the student’s question. The model’s responses are flagged as experimental and are reviewed by a human before being shown to the student, so the duck can give quick, helpful feedback without handing out full answers. | It gives students 24/7 “office‑hour” help, lets them debug code line‑by‑line, and encourages them to think through problems rather than just copy answers. |

**Key features of CS 50 Duck**

* Highlight a line of C code → “Explain this line” → instant, model‑generated explanation.  
* Highlight a block of code → “Explain changes” → shows a cleaner, more idiomatic version.  
* Ask a question about a runtime error → receives a natural‑language explanation and possible fixes.  
* The duck’s responses are accompanied by a disclaimer that it is experimental and that a human may review the answer before it is shown.  

These capabilities are described in the course’s policy and in the lecture notes on AI [1][3][9].

---

**Rules for using AI in CS 50**

| Situation | Allowed AI tools | Restrictions | Notes |
|-----------|------------------|--------------|-------|
| **Regular coursework (problem sets, labs, exams)** | **Only CS 50 Duck** (the built‑in AI helper) | External AI tools such as ChatGPT, GitHub Copilot, Bing Chat, or any other third‑party code‑generation service are **prohibited**. The policy states that these tools are “too helpful” and would give students the answers outright. | The policy is explicitly stated in the syllabus and reiterated in the lectures on AI [1][3][9]. |
| **Final project** | External AI tools **are allowed** (ChatGPT, Copilot, Bing Chat, etc.) | The project must still be your own work. You may use AI to help you write code, but you must **cite the AI** in the comments of your source files. | The final‑project guidelines make this exception clear and require citation [7]. |
| **General practice** | The CS 50 Duck can be used anytime you need help, but it will never give you a full solution to a problem set. | The duck’s responses are meant to guide you toward the answer, not to provide it directly. | This is emphasized in the policy that the duck “will help you, but not give away the entire answers to the course’s problems.” [9] |

**Bottom line**

* For everyday assignments, stick to the CS 50 Duck.  
* For the final project, you may tap into other AI tools, but you must acknowledge them in your code.  
* In all cases, the goal is to use AI as a learning aid, not a shortcut that bypasses the work you’re supposed to do.

## [Welcome!](https://cs50.harvard.edu/x/2024/notes/ai/#welcome)

- In computer science and programming circles, *rubber ducking* or *rubber duck debugging* is the act of speaking to an inanimate object to be able to *talk through* a challenging problem.
- Most recently, CS50 created our own rubber duck debugger at [cs50.ai](https://cs50.ai/) , which uses artificial intelligence as a way by which to interact with students to help them with their own challenging problems.
- Students engaging with this tool can begin understanding the potential of what AI can offer the world.

## [Image Generation](https://cs50.harvard.edu/x/2024/notes/ai/#image-generation)

- Numerous AI tools have created the potential for artificially generated images to enter the world.
- Up until recently, most of these tools had numerous tells that might indicate to an observer that an image is AI-generated.
- However, tools are becoming exceedingly good at generating these images.
- Indeed, as technology improves, it will soon be almost, if not entirely, impossible for such images to be detected with the naked eye.
- Software has also gained the ability to mutate individual images within video.

## [ChatGPT](https://cs50.harvard.edu/x/2024/notes/ai/#chatgpt)

- A very well-known bleeding-edge tool is the text generation tool *chatGPT* .
- In CS50, we do not allow the use of ChatGPT. However, we do allow the use of our own rubber duck debugger at [cs50.ai](https://cs50.ai/) .
- In CS50, we leverage the tools of Azure and OpenAI, along with our own vector database that holds very recent information from our most recent lectures and offerings, to provide our rubber duck debugger toll.

## [Prompt Generation](https://cs50.harvard.edu/x/2024/notes/ai/#prompt-generation)

- *Prompt generation* is the way by which an individual can communicate with an AI platform.
- We use a *system prompt* to teach the AI how to interact with users. We teach the AI how to work with students.
- *User prompts* are those provided by users to interact with the AI. With these prompts, students interact with the AI.

## [CS50.ai](https://cs50.harvard.edu/x/2024/notes/ai/#cs50ai)

- Our [rubber duck debugger](https://cs50.ai/) can provide conceptual help with computer science concepts.
- Further, the [rubber duck debugger](https://cs50.ai/) can help students write more efficient code.
- Additionally, the [rubber duck debugger](https://cs50.ai/) can help when a student is stuck in one of their assignments. For example, students may encounter errors that prevent them from progressing in their assignments. When students hit a wall, they don't have to wait for support staff to be available.

# [Final Project](https://cs50.harvard.edu/x/2024/project/#final-project)

The climax of this course is its final project. The final project is your opportunity to take your newfound savvy with programming out for a spin and develop your very own piece of software. So long as your project draws upon this course's lessons, the nature of your project is entirely up to you. You may implement your project in any language(s). You are welcome to utilize infrastructure other than the CS50 Codespace. All that we ask is that you build something of interest to you, that you solve an actual problem, that you impact your community, or that you change the world. Strive to create something that outlives this course.

Inasmuch as software development is rarely a one-person effort, you are allowed an opportunity to collaborate with one or two classmates for this final project. Needless to say, it is expected that every student in any such group contribute equally to the design and implementation of that group's project. Moreover, it is expected that the scope of a two- or three-person group's project be, respectively, twice or thrice that of a typical one-person project. A one-person project, mind you, should entail more time and effort than is required by each of the course's problem sets.

Note that CS50's staff audits submissions to CS50x including this final project. Students found to be in violation of [the Academic Honesty policy](..\syllabus\#academic-honesty) will be removed from the course and deemed ineligible for a certificate. Students who have already completed CS50x, if found to be in violation, will have their CS50 Certificate (and edX Certificate, if applicable) revoked.

## [Ideas](https://cs50.harvard.edu/x/2024/project/#ideas)

- a web-based application using JavaScript, Python, and SQL
- an iOS app using Swift
- a game using Lua with LÖVE
- an Android app using Java
- a Chrome extension using JavaScript
- a command-line program using C
- a hardware-based application for which you program some device
- ...

## [Getting Started](https://cs50.harvard.edu/x/2024/project/#getting-started)

Creating an entire project may seem daunting. Here are some questions that you should think about as you start:

- What will your software do? What features will it have? How will it be executed?
- What new skills will you need to acquire? What topics will you need to research?
- If working with one or two classmates, who will do what?
- In the world of software, most everything takes longer to implement than you expect. And so it's not uncommon to accomplish less in a fixed amount of time than you hope. What might you consider to be a good outcome for your project? A better outcome? The best outcome?

Consider making goal milestones to keep you on track.

If using the CS50 Codespace, create a directory called `project` to store your project source code and other files. You are welcome to develop your project outside of the CS50 Codespace.

For your final project (and your final project only!) it is reasonable to use AI-based software other than CS50's own (e.g., ChatGPT, GitHub Copilot, Bing Chat, et al.), but the essence of the work must still be your own. You've learned enough to use such tools as helpers. Treat such tools as amplifying, not supplanting, your productivity. But you still must cite any use of such tools in the comments of your code.

# [Problem Set 5](https://cs50.harvard.edu/x/2024/psets/5/#problem-set-5)

Collaboration on problem sets is not permitted except to the extent that you may ask classmates and others for help so long as that help does not reduce to another doing your work for you, per the course's policy on [academic honesty](..\..\syllabus\#academic-honesty) .

The staff conducts random audits of submissions to CS50x. Students found to be in violation of this policy will be removed from the course. Students who have already completed CS50x, if found to be in violation, will have their CS50 Certificate permanently revoked.

## [What to Do](https://cs50.harvard.edu/x/2024/psets/5/#what-to-do)

1. Log into [cs50.dev](https://cs50.dev/) using your GitHub account
2. Run `update50` in your codespace's terminal window to ensure your codespace is up-to-date and, when prompted, click **Rebuild now**
3. Submit [Inheritance](inheritance)
4. Submit [Speller](speller)

## [When to Do It](https://cs50.harvard.edu/x/2024/psets/5/#when-to-do-it)

By [2024-12-31T23:59:00-05:00](https://time.cs50.io/20241231T235900-0500) .

## [Advice](https://cs50.harvard.edu/x/2024/psets/5/#advice)

- Try out any of David's programs from [Week 5](..\..\weeks\5) .
- If you see any errors when compiling your code with `make` , focus first on fixing the very first error you see, scrolling up as needed. If unsure what it means, try asking `help50` for help. For instance, if trying to compile `speller` , and
```
make speller
```
is yielding errors, try running
```
help50 make speller
```
instead!
